sections.title: Data Engineering and ML Pipeline Cost by Project Type — 2025
sections.description: Cost ranges, timelines, and primary cost drivers for the most common data engineering and ML pipeline projects.

sections.title: What Drives Data Engineering Cost
sections.description: Number of data sources, data quality work, real-time vs. batch, feature store, and MLOps scope — each significantly impacts your total investment.

items.title: 1. Number and Complexity of Data Sources
items.description: Each additional data source adds integration scope. Well-documented REST API: $3,000–$8,000. Database extraction: $4,000–$10,000. SAP/Oracle ERP: $8,000–$20,000. Legacy system: $5,000–$15,000. Streaming source: $8,000–$18,000. Third-party SaaS: $6,000–$15,000.
items.label: Data Sources

items.title: 2. Data Quality Work
items.description: Raw enterprise data is almost never analysis-ready. Missing values (<5% fields): $2,000–$5,000. Missing values (>20% key fields): $8,000–$20,000. Schema inconsistency: $5,000–$15,000. Duplicate resolution: $8,000–$20,000. Historical label backfill: $10,000–$30,000.
items.label: Data Quality

items.title: 3. Real-Time vs. Batch Processing
items.description: Batch processing (daily/hourly): lower cost, Airflow/dbt. Real-time streaming (sub-second latency): Kafka/Kinesis/Flink, adds $20,000–$40,000 over batch for infrastructure complexity. Necessary for fraud detection, real-time recommendations, operational monitoring.
items.label: Processing Mode

items.title: 4. Feature Store vs. Ad-Hoc Engineering
items.description: Without feature store: each model builds own logic, faster initially but creates training-serving skew. With feature store (Feast/Hopsworks/custom): $30,000–$75,000. Eliminates entire class of production ML problems. Pays off when building 4+ models sharing features.
items.label: Feature Store

items.title: 5. MLOps Infrastructure Scope
items.description: Minimal (experiment tracking only): $20,000–$40,000. Standard (CI/CD + drift monitoring + retraining): $40,000–$80,000. Full platform (all components): $80,000–$250,000. Right scope depends on model count and production requirements.
items.label: MLOps Scope

sections.title: The Cost of Not Investing in Data Engineering
sections.description: Organizations that skip data engineering investment and jump straight to ML model development consistently encounter these expensive problems.

items.title: Training-Serving Skew
items.description: The model's training features and production serving features are computed differently. The model appears to work in training but underperforms in production. Diagnosis and remediation typically costs 2–3× what a proper feature store would have cost to build initially.
items.label: Skew

items.title: Manual Retraining Cycles
items.description: Without automated retraining pipelines, every model update requires a manual data engineering sprint. For organizations with 5+ production models, this becomes a continuous bottleneck consuming disproportionate data science time.
items.label: Manual Retraining

items.title: Undetected Data Quality Drift
items.description: Source schema changes, upstream data pipeline failures, and distribution shifts that go unmonitored cause silent model degradation — the model starts making worse decisions, but nobody notices until the business metric impact becomes visible weeks later.
items.label: Drift

items.title: Data Lineage Gaps
items.description: Unable to answer 'which training data produced which model version?' — a requirement for regulated industries (SR 26-2, HIPAA, EU AI Act) and increasingly a general governance expectation.
items.label: Lineage Gaps

items.title: Why is data engineering so expensive relative to the ML models?
items.description: Because it's genuinely harder in enterprise environments than model development. Production data pipelines handle schema drift, source system outages, data quality variance, and incremental updates in ways that notebook-based data loading for model training doesn't. The engineering required is substantial.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.description: Common questions about data engineering and ML pipeline development costs.

items.question: Should we invest in a feature store or is it overkill?
items.answer: If you're building 1–3 models with distinct feature sets, feature store overhead isn't justified. For 4+ models sharing features, or if you've already experienced training-serving skew, a feature store investment pays back in reduced debugging time and higher production model accuracy.

items.question: What's the difference between dbt and Airflow for data pipelines?
items.answer: dbt transforms data within your warehouse (SQL-based, version-controlled, tested transformations); Airflow orchestrates when and in what order pipeline tasks run. They're complementary — most modern data stacks use both. ClickMasters selects the right tool combination for your specific architecture.

items.question: Can data engineering work with our existing Snowflake/Databricks investment?
items.answer: Yes — ClickMasters builds directly on your existing warehouse infrastructure rather than introducing new platforms where your existing investment is sound.

items.question: How long does a full MLOps platform take to build?
items.answer: 16–32 weeks for a comprehensive MLOps platform. ClickMasters recommends phased delivery: experiment tracking first (6–8 weeks), then CI/CD and monitoring (additional 8–12 weeks), then advanced features.

items.question: What ongoing maintenance does data engineering require after delivery?
items.answer: Pipeline monitoring response, schema change handling as source systems evolve, and capacity scaling as data volumes grow. ClickMasters offers monthly support contracts covering routine pipeline maintenance.

items.question: Can ClickMasters take over an existing data pipeline that's not working?
items.answer: Yes — pipeline audits and remediation are a specific engagement type. ClickMasters diagnoses what's failing and either remediates or recommends a targeted rebuild.
